content: During previous visits, the patient received detailed counseling and education regarding their condition, including discussions about family planning, pregnancy, contraception, and tuberculosis (TB) status. These aspects were reviewed at each visit. Laboratory tests requested during the last visit and the patient’s prior experience with antiretroviral therapy (ART) were also documented. Programs should aim to minimize the number of patients lost to follow-up by ensuring timely diagnosis and establishing strong connections between testing facilities and treatment initiation. Patients who are lost to follow-up (LTF) require special attention. Community-based health workers play a critical role in tracking these patients and understanding the reasons for their disengagement from care. These workers can facilitate re-engagement with care services, ideally soon after a missed appointment. Once the true outcome of these patients is determined, they can generally be reclassified as deceased, having stopped ART, or having transferred care (either formally or informally). Patients who transfer in (TI) or out (TO) of facilities pose additional challenges in settings without unique patient identifiers or when they present without their health records. Double-counting is inevitable in such cases if patients receive care at multiple facilities during the same period without the use of unique identifiers. Ideally, a primary facility should monitor the patient’s care and treatment outcomes. Stable patients and those with advanced disease require clear definitions to support the sustained scale-up of ART. Consolidated guidelines emphasize the importance of person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance. Accurate patient records are essential for ensuring the quality of care, avoiding incorrect drug regimens, and preventing patients from being mistakenly counted as new when they have already been enrolled in care and started on ART. Clinical teams must summarize data from patient groups to improve care planning, coordination, and management, as well as to ensure the proper ordering of medications and supplies. Integrated patient monitoring tools are critical for linking services such as TB treatment, family planning, and maternal health services. These tools ensure comprehensive patient management over time. For example, ART should be initiated and maintained in pregnant and postpartum women and infants within maternal and child health (MCH) settings. ART and TB treatment should also be provided in settings where both conditions are managed. Unique patient identifiers, if used, should be assigned to facilitate accurate record-keeping and data reconciliation across services. Family charts or folders can be used to consolidate records for members of the same household, which is particularly useful for mother-infant pairs and integrated family care. Appointment systems or linked pharmacy and clinical records can help identify patients who miss scheduled visits, enabling timely follow-up. Data reconciliation across registers (e.g., ART, antenatal care [ANC], labor and delivery [L&D], HIV-exposed infant [HEI], and TB) is essential for comprehensive care. Innovative approaches to integrating patient records in both paper and electronic formats are being adopted in various settings. For instance, South Africa’s Western Cape Province has introduced a single patient record system, while Malawi has integrated non-communicable disease and antenatal care modules within its HIV electronic medical records system. Longitudinal registers that integrate ART records with those for non-HIV-related treatment and care may be more complex to implement but are essential for comprehensive patient management. In settings where patients receive care at both HIV and TB clinics, cross-referencing patient identifiers (e.g., HIV patient card numbers and TB registration numbers) allows for better linkage of records across programs. Patient-held cards, booklets, or passports containing appointment dates and clinical information can also facilitate record linkage across service delivery points. National databases should prioritize the use of unique identifiers over names to enhance data confidentiality and security. The use of HIV patient cards is recommended for all confirmed HIV-positive patients enrolled in care and starting ART, particularly in MCH and TB settings. ART registers should also be used in these settings. Minimum recommended data elements for HIV patient-held cards include the patient’s name, date of birth, unique ID (if available), ART point of care, ART start date, ARV regimen details, and laboratory results such as CD4 count and viral load. Efforts to eliminate mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV require comprehensive interventions integrated into essential MCH services. These include the prevention of HIV infection among women of reproductive age, prevention of unintended pregnancies among HIV-infected women, prevention of HIV transmission during pregnancy, delivery, and breastfeeding, and provision of care and treatment for HIV-infected women and their families. Pregnant women living with HIV should be linked to MCH/PMTCT services and have their care documented on HIV patient cards. Special attention should be given to following the mother-infant pair through the cascade of care, from ANC to postpartum visits and child health clinics. Monitoring systems should support the integration of PMTCT and pediatric HIV care with MCH services. This includes capturing cross-referrals and ensuring timely provision of PMTCT interventions. For example, HEI registers should follow the entire cascade of care for exposed infants, capturing all relevant interventions and outcomes. Longitudinal MIP registers may also be used to document PMTCT interventions for HIV-positive mothers and their infants. WHO guidelines recommend increasing the minimum number of ANC contacts during pregnancy to improve perinatal outcomes and women’s care experiences. Differentiated care models for HIV-positive women on ART who become pregnant may involve more frequent contacts during ANC and fewer postpartum. Service providers should aim to meet the recommended minimum number of contacts for both ANC and HIV care to ensure optimal outcomes for mothers and infants. Data elements relevant to HIV care and treatment for pregnant and postpartum women and their newborns should be included in maternal health cards, labor and postpartum records, ANC and L&D registers, and child health cards. These elements include enrollment dates, unique IDs, ART start dates, ARV regimens, visit dates, weight, CD4 counts, and prophylaxis details. This version maintains the technical and detailed nature of the original text while ensuring clarity and readability for medical professionals.
